readerTitle: Your supplier just raised prices. Who wins the next ten rounds?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (철물점과 유통업체, 배관 업체와 도매상) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 오래 거래한 공급업체와의 협상은 한 번의 가격 싸움이 아니라 반복되는 게임의 한 판이다. 미래 관계를 지키면서, 내 대안과 약속은 믿을 수 있게 만든다.
misconception: 협상은 이번 가격을 최대한 깎는 것이고, '다른 데로 옮기겠다'는 말만으로도 압박이 된다.

sources.text: Axelrod, R. (1984). The Evolution of Cooperation. Basic Books. ('the shadow of the future')
게임이론의 표준 개념 (반복 게임, 신뢰할 수 있는 약속)
모든 수치와 인물은 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 계산 확인: 연간 구매액 $200,000 × 6% = $12,000. 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 수치입니다.
'the shadow of the future' 표현이 Axelrod(1984)에서 쓰인 것이 맞는지 게시 전 원문으로 확인하세요.

cards.title: Your supplier of six years just raised prices 6%.
body: Maria runs two hardware stores. She buys about $200,000 a year from one regional distributor. This morning's email says prices go up 6% next month. That's $12,000 a year.
Her first instinct is to fight. Before she replies, it helps to see what game she's actually playing.

image.label: Store owner reading a price-increase email at the counter
image.brief: 따뜻한 일러스트. 동네 철물점 계산대에서 주인이 노트북 화면의 'Price update: +6%' 이메일을 보고 있음. 뒤 선반에 페인트와 공구. 실제 브랜드나 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: How should Maria reply?
body: A rival distributor once quoted her lower prices on paint and fasteners, but she never placed an order. Her current distributor delivers on time and gave her stock first during last winter's shortage.

options.text: Tell them a rival is cheaper and she'll switch unless they drop the increase
options.feedback: A threat only works if it's believable. She's never bought from the rival, and they may know it. If they call the bluff, she backs down or switches to an untested supplier. That's **credible commitments** at work.

options.text: Accept part of the increase in exchange for something lasting, like a 12-month price lock and first call on stock
options.feedback: She treats this as one round in a long game. Giving a little now buys stability and protects the goodwill that got her stock in the shortage. That's **repeated games** at work.

options.text: Accept the full 6% quietly to keep the relationship warm
options.feedback: It protects goodwill, but it teaches the distributor she'll pay whatever is asked. In a **repeated game**, the other side learns from every round, including this one.

cards.title: This isn't one deal. It's round seven.
body: A one-time buyer should push for the lowest price and walk away. Maria isn't a one-time buyer. She'll order from this distributor every week for years.

In that kind of game, price is only part of what's on the table. The rest is harder to see: who gets stock in a shortage, who gets longer payment terms, who hears about a price rise early. Squeezing hard today can win this round and lose the next ten.

cards.title: Tomorrow keeps today honest.
body: In a **repeated game**, the same players meet again and again. Each side cooperates now because it wants the other side to cooperate later. Political scientist Robert Axelrod called this *the shadow of the future*. The longer it falls, the more cooperation pays.
For Maria, that means judging each offer by what it does to future rounds. A fair deal she can repeat is worth more than a great deal that sours the relationship.

image.label: A long road of handshakes stretching into the distance
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 왼쪽에서 오른쪽으로 이어지는 타임라인 위에 'Round 1'부터 'Round 10'까지 작은 악수 아이콘. 현재 'Round 7'만 강조되고, 뒤쪽 라운드 위에 길게 드리운 그림자 표현. 로고 없음.

cards.title: A threat is only as good as your backup plan.
body: Saying "I'll switch" costs nothing, so suppliers often ignore it. A **credible commitment** is one the other side believes because you've made it real or costly to back out of.

Maria can make her outside option real by placing small, regular orders with the rival on one product line. Now switching is a tested path, not a bluff. Commitments can help her, too. Promising a year of volume is something the distributor can bank on, so it's worth a better price.
cards.softwareNote: The same game plays out when a software company renews with its cloud or data vendor. A multi-year spend commitment is the usual way to earn a discount, and having tested a second provider makes "we could move" believable.

cards.title: Now it's a plumbing company.
body: Dev runs a home plumbing firm. His local wholesaler offers 5% off water heaters and parts if he signs a two-year exclusive deal. A second wholesaler across town is sometimes faster when a job is urgent. What's the smartest reply?

image.label: Plumber's van between two parts wholesalers
image.brief: 배관 작업 밴 한 대가 가운데 있고, 왼쪽에 큰 도매상 창고('2-year exclusive: 5% off' 말풍선), 오른쪽에 작은 도매상('Fast pickup' 말풍선). 실제 상호나 로고 없음.

options.text: Sign the two-year exclusive and take the 5%
options.feedback: The discount is real, but exclusivity removes his walk-away option. With no **credible** way to leave, he loses leverage on delivery times and the next price change.

options.text: Decline and buy from whoever is cheapest each week
options.feedback: He keeps flexibility, but neither wholesaler has a reason to put him first. Without a **repeated** relationship, there's no future to earn priority with.

options.text: Commit most of his volume for one year, with a delivery-time standard, and keep a small account across town
options.feedback: His volume promise is a **credible commitment** worth a discount. The small second account keeps his outside option real. Both concepts work at once.

cards.title: Cooperation needs a future.
body: Repeated games only hold when both sides expect to keep playing. If a supplier is being sold, closing a product line, or you plan to leave, the shadow of the future shrinks. Each side starts grabbing what it can now. Watch for those signs and get key terms in writing.
Loyalty also isn't a reason to stop checking. Get an outside quote every year or so. You may never use it, but it keeps your sense of a fair price and your backup plan up to date.

cards.title: With a long-term supplier, negotiate the relationship, not just the price.
body: The two ideas this lesson put to work:
list: **Repeated games:** judge each deal by what it does to future rounds
**Credible commitments:** make your walk-away option real, and offer promises the other side can bank on
cards.callout: **Try it today:** pick your biggest supplier. Write down one thing besides price you'd want for a longer commitment, and one small step that would make your backup option real.
